title: Japan closes 2.85% lower as the 3% yield shock spreads
summary: Tokyo's selloff deepened into the close: the Nikkei finished at 64,325.64, down 2.85%, while TOPIX lost 2.40% and the 10-year JGB yield stayed around 3.01%. The earlier bond-and-oil warning is now a full-session event, not just an opening shock.
why_it_matters: The weakness became broad enough to hit the wider market, not only expensive technology shares. Japan is facing a difficult mix of high oil, high sovereign yields and still-weak currency levels, which can pressure both household import costs and equity valuations.

claims.text: The Nikkei 225 closed September 2 at 64,325.64, down 1,889.70 points or 2.85%.
claims.basis: Official Nikkei close cross-checked with market reporting.

claims.text: TOPIX closed at 4,081.60, down 100.26 points or 2.40%, while the new 10-year JGB yield was around 3.01% in the Tokyo session.
claims.basis: Tokyo market close data reported independently by OANDA and Xinhua.

claims.text: Xinhua reported that all Tokyo market sectors declined, showing the weakness had broadened beyond a narrow group of growth stocks.
claims.basis: Closing market breadth reported by Xinhua.

claims.text: Global markets were simultaneously dealing with higher oil prices and a deeper sovereign-bond selloff amid renewed U.S.-Iran hostilities.
Because the decline broadened into TOPIX and across sectors while JGB yields stayed above 3%, the September 2 move looks more like a cross-asset discount-rate shock than a technology-only correction.
claims.basis: Inference from breadth, index performance and concurrent bond/oil moves.

claims.text: ALAM's earlier September 2 negative opening and intraday risk calls were directionally correct through the cash-market close.
claims.basis: Archived ALAM forecast compared with verified closing direction.

content.key_message: The September 2 stress signal survived the entire session and broadened across Tokyo equities.

change_summary.previous: At 14:13 ALAM recorded an intraday Nikkei decline of about 2.6% and said the close had not yet tested whether the stress would persist.
change_summary.now: The Nikkei closed down 2.85%, TOPIX lost 2.40%, the 10-year JGB yield remained around 3.01%, and reported sector breadth was uniformly negative.
change_summary.why_change_matters: The stress persisted and broadened, strengthening the case that the move is tied to the rates/oil regime rather than a brief opening-position unwind.

content.what_moved: Nikkei 64,325.64 (-2.85%); TOPIX 4,081.60 (-2.40%); 10-year JGB about 3.01%; USD/JPY around 159.81 in the Tokyo digest.
why_it_moved: Renewed Middle East hostilities kept crude oil and inflation risk elevated.
Japanese and global sovereign yields stayed high, increasing the discount rate applied to equities.
The selloff broadened across sectors, showing the pressure was not confined to one theme.
content.japan_transmission: High oil raises import-cost pressure; high JGB yields raise financing and valuation pressure; a weak yen can still help some exporters but simultaneously worsens imported energy and food costs.
content.breadth_and_sectors: The closing evidence points to broad weakness: TOPIX fell 2.40% and Xinhua reported all sectors lower. That is more concerning than a narrow high-growth selloff because it indicates a wider repricing of risk.
content.fx_rates_cross_asset: The key cross-asset cluster remains oil up, sovereign yields high, equities down and the yen still near historically weak levels despite some intraday strengthening.
content.fundamental_vs_positioning: The oil and yield changes are observable macro inputs. Positioning and futures hedging can amplify daily moves, so the 2.85% decline alone does not prove a new long-term bear market.
content.bull_case: A credible geopolitical de-escalation that pulls oil and global yields down could quickly relieve the valuation squeeze and turn the move into a sharp but temporary reset.
content.bear_case: If oil remains elevated and Japanese yields continue rising from above 3%, the pressure can migrate from valuation into earnings, household purchasing power and financing conditions.
content.market_pricing_inference: INFERENCE: Tokyo is increasingly pricing the geopolitical shock through inflation and interest rates, not only through a short-lived fear premium.
content.opening_bias: Completed: NEGATIVE bias was directionally correct.
content.forecast_next_session: VOLATILE / DOWNSIDE-RISK while both oil and sovereign yields remain elevated. A strong overnight reversal in either would soften the call.
content.forecast_5d: Expect large swings around oil, JGB/Treasury yields, BOJ communication and U.S. macro data. A durable rebound needs at least one major pressure channel to ease.
content.forecast_1_3m: Japan equities can remain fundamentally supported by earnings only if higher rates and energy costs do not materially compress margins or valuations. Persistent 3%+ JGB yields would make that test harder.
catalysts: Brent and WTI direction after the U.S.-Iran escalation
Japan 10-year JGB behavior above the 3% area
BOJ communication before the September 17-18 meeting
U.S. Treasury yields and Federal Reserve expectations
Whether Tokyo breadth stabilizes in the next session
content.practical_guidelines: Do not treat one red day as a reason to chase or panic. Watch whether oil and yields remain high together; that combination matters more for the regime than the headline index percentage by itself.
content.what_would_change_mind: A sustained fall in oil and sovereign yields with improving Tokyo breadth would weaken the downside thesis. Further increases in yields accompanied by another broad equity decline would strengthen it.

Bottom line: the morning downside signal was confirmed through the close.
reading_levels.2_min: The earlier September 2 ALAM market warning is now fully testable: the Nikkei ended down 2.85% and TOPIX down 2.40%, with the 10-year JGB yield still around 3.01%. Reported sector breadth was broadly negative. That combination matters because Japan is dealing with higher energy costs and a higher discount-rate environment at the same time. A weak yen can support exporter translation earnings, but it also increases import pressure. The next-session call stays volatile/downside-risk unless oil or yields reverse materially overnight.
